bull_thesis: The bull case is that Bausch + Lomb is a genuinely improving eye-health franchise trading at a discount created almost entirely by who owns it, and that the discount closes when that owner finally leaves. Bausch Health held 310,449,643 shares, about 87% of the company, as of 22 July 2026. That leaves a free float of roughly 47 million shares out of 357 million - too small for index funds and most institutions, which caps the multiple regardless of results. Strip the overhang away and you own a business that, in the second quarter of 2026 reported on 29 July, grew revenue about 8% on a constant-currency basis to $1.394 billion (an acceleration from 6% in the first quarter), with all three segments growing and both surgical and pharmaceuticals up double digits. Adjusted gross margin rose 160 basis points to 62.2%; adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) rose 28% to $246 million, a 17.6% margin, up 260 basis points. Management raised full-year guidance for the second time this year, to $5.44-$5.54 billion of revenue and $1.025-$1.075 billion of adjusted EBITDA. Net leverage fell a full turn year-over-year to 4.7 times. At $16.91 the shares carry an enterprise value near $10.8 billion against $4.76 billion of net debt, or roughly 10.3 times guided 2026 adjusted EBITDA - against eye-care and medical-technology peers in the mid-teens. The November 2025 investor day laid out 5-7% constant-currency revenue growth per year through 2028, an adjusted EBITDA margin near 23% in 2028, double-digit adjusted earnings-per-share growth, and net leverage near 3.5 times by the end of 2028. That plan puts 2028 adjusted EBITDA near $1.4 billion. Conditions the bull case needs: the parent actually completes the separation rather than optioning it for another cycle; the launch-driven growth holds at the 5-7% pace; margin expansion continues so the leverage gate is reached; and the eventual share distribution is absorbed without a prolonged supply overhang. Meet those and a clean, deleveraging pure-play at 12 times 2027 adjusted EBITDA is worth roughly $27 a share.
bear_thesis: The bear case is that we are paying a full price for an undated option, and that the option costs us money when it is finally exercised. Bausch Health has been promising this separation since August 2020. It announced a spin-off and did not deliver one; it carved out 35 million shares in a May 2022 initial public offering instead; it ran a full sale process in 2024 and announced in February 2025 that the process was complete and would not result in a transaction. Six years, three routes, and the stake is essentially where it started. The current filings say only that the parent 'continues to evaluate' a distribution, a sale, or a combination, expressly conditioned on 'the achievement of targeted debt leverage ratios and the receipt of any applicable shareholder and other necessary approvals' - with the warning that approvals may not be obtained 'on the terms or timelines anticipated or at all.' On the 29 July 2026 call the parent's chief financial officer declined to name either a structure or a date, and noted that the 2025 refinancing had 'extended the runway' and increased 'flexibility around the timing and the process.' The parent has bought itself the right to wait, and it will use it. Worse, the flow cuts the wrong way first: distributing 310 million shares to Bausch Health's own holders delivers roughly six times the current free float into a shareholder base that bought a leveraged pharmaceutical company, not an eye-health growth stock. The supply clears before the re-rating, so an investor who buys today pays a pre-event price and then absorbs the selling. Meanwhile the balance sheet does not forgive delay: $5,128 million of debt principal against $367 million of cash at a 7.43% blended rate, with roughly $365 million of interest expense guided for 2026 - more than a third of adjusted EBITDA - $1.4 billion of senior secured notes due 2028, free cash flow of only $90 million in the quarter against roughly $285 million of annual capital expenditure, and a trailing-twelve-month net loss of $171 million. interrogator_dossier:
# Bausch + Lomb (BLCO) - Forensic Dossier on the Event

Prepared 3 August 2026. All prices and filings verified against public sources dated on or before 31 July 2026.

The question in front of us is not whether Bausch + Lomb is a good eye-health company. It is whether a specific corporate event - the unwinding of Bausch Health's roughly 87% ownership stake - is real, dated, and binding enough to pay us for the risk of owning the shares at $16.91.

The short answer: the event is real, it has been real for six years, and it still has no date.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC - six years of intention, no completion

The separation story begins in August 2020, when Bausch Health announced its intention to spin off its eye-health business into an independent public company. What actually happened was smaller: in May 2022, a Bausch Health subsidiary sold 35 million shares of Bausch + Lomb in an initial public offering. That created a listed stock with a very thin free float and left the parent holding the overwhelming majority of the equity.

From there the story changed shape twice more rather than progressing. Through 2022-2024 the route was a spin-off: the parent said the remaining stake would be distributed to its own shareholders once leverage targets were met, and it was not. In late 2024 the route became a sale - after rumours moved the stock, the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization required a disclosure and the company confirmed it was exploring a sale of the whole company to a third party. In February 2025 that route closed with nothing: the company announced that after engaging with potential buyers, the process was complete and would not result in a transaction. The shares fell on the news and Bausch Health kept its stake. Through 2026 the language returned to open-ended evaluation, in both companies' quarterly filings and on both management calls of 29 July 2026.

The pattern matters more than any single step. Each time the route has changed, the destination has stayed the same and the arrival time has moved. That is the single most important fact in this file.

## 2. THE EVENT, TESTED - is it dated and binding?

As of the quarter ended 30 June 2026, Bausch Health directly or indirectly held 310,449,643 Bausch + Lomb common shares - approximately 87% of shares outstanding as of 22 July 2026. The parent 'continues to evaluate completing a separation, which could involve a distribution to its shareholders, a sale transaction, or a combination.' Completion is expressly conditioned on 'the achievement of targeted debt leverage ratios and the receipt of any applicable shareholder and other necessary approvals,' with the filing warning that approvals may not be obtained 'on the terms or timelines anticipated or at all.'

Tested against the three things a hard catalyst needs: a date is absent (no timeline in either quarterly filing; neither management team offered one on 29 July 2026); a binding obligation is absent (no agreement, no offer, no contractual payout - a stated intention only); and a named structure is absent (distribution, sale, or combination all still on the table).

On the parent's 29 July 2026 call, the chief financial officer said the company is 'evaluating multiple ways to translate that asset's value into Bausch Health's share price' and added: 'There are obviously a number of considerations to evaluate and to figure out exactly how do we translate the value of B+L into a BHC share price, and we're looking at all and any avenues to do so.' He pointed to the 2025 refinancing as having 'extended the runway' and increased 'flexibility around the timing and the process.' Flexibility around timing is, from our seat, the opposite of a catalyst. Bausch + Lomb's own management has been candid that this is not theirs to solve, describing the majority-share overhang as 'not within our control' and 'a BHC issue.'

One thing genuinely did move. The gating condition - leverage - is closing. Bausch Health cut net debt by $434 million in the June quarter to roughly $13.7 billion against total borrowings of about $20.2 billion. Bausch + Lomb's own net leverage (net debt divided by adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) fell a full turn year-over-year to 4.7 times, against a stated target of about 3.5 times by the end of 2028. So the door is being unlocked. The published target date for reaching that leverage level is end-2028, which is the closest thing to a date this situation has, and it is more than two years out.

## 3. THE SPONSOR'S CREDIBILITY

Bausch Health is the only party who can fire this catalyst, and its record on this specific promise is poor: one announced spin-off not delivered (2020), one partial carve-out delivered instead (2022), one full sale process run and abandoned (2024-25). Three attempts, six years, stake essentially unchanged at 88% then and roughly 87% now - the drift is share-count dilution at the subsidiary, not selling by the parent.

The mitigating evidence is operational rather than transactional. Under chief executive Brent Saunders, Bausch + Lomb is executing well: second-quarter 2026 revenue of $1.394 billion beat the roughly $1.37 billion consensus and grew about 8% on a constant-currency basis (a pick-up from 6% in the first quarter), with all three segments growing and surgical and pharmaceuticals both up double digits. Adjusted gross margin rose 160 basis points to 62.2%; adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation rose 28% to $246 million, a 17.6% margin, up 260 basis points. Full-year 2026 guidance was raised to $5.44-$5.54 billion of revenue and $1.025-$1.075 billion of adjusted earnings. At a November 2025 investor day the company set out targets of 5-7% constant-currency revenue growth per year through 2028, roughly 23% adjusted margin in 2028, double-digit adjusted earnings-per-share growth from 2026 to 2028, and net leverage near 3.5 times by end-2028.

So: high credibility on running the business, low credibility on delivering the transaction. Those are two different scores, and only the second one is the thesis.

## 4. THE DOWNSIDE FLOOR - what actually backstops the price?

This is where the setup is weakest. There is no contractual floor. This is not a merger with a signed agreement, so there is no deal-break price. There is no cash pile - the company holds $367 million of cash against $5,128 million of debt principal, roughly $4.76 billion net, at a 7.43% weighted average interest rate. There is no reverse termination fee, no contingent value right, no tender at a fixed price. Nothing pays us if the event does not happen.

What exists instead is a valuation floor and a price memory. On valuation: at the low end of 2026 guidance ($1.025 billion of adjusted earnings), about 8.5 times enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation implies an enterprise value near $8.7 billion; less $4.76 billion of net debt, that is roughly $11.80 per share, while nine times gets you to about $13.10. On price memory: the 52-week range is $13.09 to $18.92, the shares troughed in that low-$13s area, and traded lower still during the spring-2025 risk-off episode.

So the $11.80 figure our board carries is a stress-case valuation, not a backstop - and it sits below the 52-week low, meaning it has not been tested in the past year. Note also the leverage arithmetic: with net debt roughly 44% of enterprise value, a 15% cut to the earnings estimate takes about 27% off the equity. Debt makes the floor softer than it looks, not harder.

## 5. RED FLAGS

The catalyst, if it fires, hurts first. This is the most under-appreciated point in the file. The forced-seller mechanic works in both directions. If the parent distributes 310 million shares to its own shareholders, those shares land with a holder base that bought a leveraged, litigation-scarred pharmaceutical company - not an eye-health growth stock. Roughly six times the current free float would be delivered into unwilling hands. The supply clears before the re-rating, not after. Buying today means paying a pre-event price and then eating the flow.

Beyond that: the company is still unprofitable on a reported basis, with a trailing-twelve-month net loss of $171 million (loss per share of $0.48) and a first-half 2026 net loss of $85 million, improved from $274 million a year earlier - adjusted earnings are the only earnings. Leverage is heavy: net debt of about $4.76 billion at 4.7 times, with $1.4 billion of senior secured notes due 2028 and a $2.795 billion term loan due 2031 at a blended 7.43%, and interest expense guidance of roughly $365 million for 2026 consuming more than a third of adjusted earnings. Free cash flow is thin at $90 million in the second quarter against capital expenditure guided near $285 million for the year; year-to-date conversion of about 46% is real progress but leaves little room for error. And this is a controlled company with no independent path - minority holders cannot force the outcome. The parent decides, on the parent's timetable, in the parent's interest, and the parent's interest is its own $20 billion debt stack, not our entry price.

## 6. GREEN FLAGS

Revenue growth is accelerating (6% to 8% constant currency between the first and second quarters of 2026) with all segments contributing. Margins expanded 260 basis points at the adjusted earnings line and guidance has been raised twice this year. Leverage is down a full turn year-over-year at both the subsidiary and the parent - the exact condition the transaction is gated on. Valuation is genuinely undemanding at roughly 10.3 times enterprise value to 2026 guided adjusted earnings, against eye-care and medical-technology peers in the mid-teens; much of that gap is the overhang itself, which is the point of the trade. And the franchise is real: a recognised brand with about 170 years of history, plus regulatory approvals and surgeon habit in intraocular lenses and contact lenses that make it hard to displace quickly, even as a distant number three behind Alcon and Johnson & Johnson Vision in most categories.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The parent has quietly stopped promising and started optioning. The language moved from 'intends to spin off' (2020) to 'may include monetization of all or a portion' (2026) - that is a widening of the option set, which reads as flexibility to management and as slippage to us. The refinancing that 'extended the runway' removed the very pressure that would have forced the sale; the parent bought itself the right to wait, and it will use it. Meanwhile the subsidiary's investor-day targets run to 2028, and the parent named those targets as 'an important consideration' in choosing among options - which is a polite way of saying the parent would rather sell a company hitting its 2028 plan than one still proving it.

## 8. VERDICT FOR THE DIRECTOR

Classification: the operating business is strengthening; the event is stalled. Treat those separately and do not let the first pay for the second.

The single thing to weigh before sizing: this is a valuation position wearing a catalyst costume. Everything genuinely attractive here - 10.3 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation on an accelerating franchise, expanding margins, falling leverage - is a value case that would stand on its own. The catalyst adds no date, no binding term, and no protection, and when it eventually fires it will deliver roughly six free floats of supply into the market before it delivers a re-rating. The price is not distressed either: at $16.91 the shares sit above both the 50-day ($15.93) and 200-day ($16.34) averages and in the upper half of the 52-week range, roughly 43% above the notional stress floor. We would be paying a normal price for an undated option and calling it asymmetry.

On the two secondary dimensions: the moat is narrow but real - brand and regulatory approvals in lenses and surgical implants, with switching friction among surgeons - and it is holding rather than eroding, given the margin expansion. No structural force threatens the terminal value; an ageing population is a tailwind for eye health, with only modest reimbursement pressure on the surgical and pharmaceutical lines. Neither dimension is what decides this name.

Clear the block and three things happen at once - the float multiplies roughly eight-fold, index eligibility widens, and the overhang that has capped the multiple disappears. On the way there, a buyer might simply take the whole company, which is close to what nearly happened: in autumn 2024 TPG and Blackstone worked on a joint bid reported at $13-14 billion, roughly $25 a share, with Goldman Sachs running the process. The parent's own incentive has never been sharper: Bausch Health's entire market value is about $2.1 billion while its stake in Bausch + Lomb is worth roughly $5.2 billion, so the rest of the parent is being valued at less than nothing - an untenable position that only a separation resolves. # Bausch + Lomb (BLCO) - Event Dossier
## The forced-divestiture thesis, tested against the record
### Prepared 27 July 2026 | live price $16.28 | board target $26.97 | board floor $11.80

## 1. THE EVENT, STATED PLAINLY

Bausch + Lomb is an eye-care company - contact lenses, lens-care solutions, dry-eye drugs and cataract-surgery equipment - that generated roughly $5.2 billion of revenue over the twelve months to March 2026. It is about 87-88% owned by its parent, Bausch Health Companies, which held 310,449,643 of the 356.5 million shares outstanding as of 22 April 2026. Only some 46 million shares - worth about $750 million at today's price of $16.28 - trade freely.

The thesis on our board is not that this is a great business. It is that the parent must eventually sell or hand out that block, and that when the block clears, the share price stops carrying the discount a controlled, thin-float stock always carries. Our board entry frames this as forced-seller supply clearing, with a target of $26.97 against a floor of $11.80.

My job is to ask whether that event is real, whether it is dated, and whether the floor is anything more than a hopeful number. The short answer: the event is real in intent and entirely unscheduled in fact; the pressure that would have forced it has been defused; two legal gates stand in front of the cleanest route; and the floor is a valuation opinion rather than a backstop.

The arc is the finding. Every year the sponsor restates the goal, and every year the goal recedes. The one time the process reached the price-discovery stage - autumn 2024 into February 2025 - it failed at the point where a buyer had to write a cheque.

In April 2023 Judge Margaret Goodzeit largely denied the motion to dismiss and upheld the plaintiffs' right to enjoin a dividend of Bausch + Lomb shares. A preliminary injunction was denied in December 2022 as premature, expressly subject to renewal if the parent takes concrete steps toward the distribution. In plain terms: the specific mechanism this thesis needs can be blocked by injunction the moment it is attempted, and no 2026 trial date is publicly scheduled.

## 4. THE SPONSOR'S CREDIBILITY

The sponsor is the parent, and its record on this specific promise is poor: six years of stated intent, one public failure, no date. That is not deception - the strategic logic has always been sound and the obstacles were real. But for an investor buying a spread that only closes when the event fires, intent without a clock is worth very little.

Set against that, the operating management of Bausch + Lomb itself has been delivering. The first quarter of 2026 showed revenue of $1.244 billion, up $107 million or 9% on the prior year, with adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (excluding acquired research charges) of $200 million against $126 million a year earlier - a 59% increase, a 16.1% margin. The company raised full-year guidance to revenue of $5.42-5.52 billion and adjusted earnings of $1.010-1.060 billion, the second raise in five months. Guidance credibility at the operating level: High. Event credibility at the parent level: Low. Those are two different scores and should not be blended.

One striking cross-check on the parent's incentives: Bausch Health's own market value is about $2.1 billion, while its 88% stake in Bausch + Lomb is worth roughly $5.2 billion at the current price. The parent trades at a deeply negative stub - the market values everything else it owns, net of debt, at less than nothing. That is simultaneously the strongest argument that the parent eventually must act, and a warning that the market does not believe the stake can be extracted cleanly.

## 5. THE FLOOR - WHAT ACTUALLY BACKSTOPS $11.80?

Nothing hard. In a genuine special situation the floor is an asset: cash, a break fee, a recovery claim, a signed alternative bid. Bausch + Lomb has none of these. It held $279 million of cash against $5.07 billion of total debt at 31 March 2026 - net debt of roughly $4.80 billion, about 4.6 times this year's expected adjusted earnings. Reported earnings are still negative: a net loss of $71 million in the first quarter and roughly $219 million over the trailing year, on $4.74 billion of goodwill.

So $11.80 is not a backstop. It is a multiple - roughly 8.5 to 9 times this year's adjusted earnings - and it is reachable. Because the equity is levered 4.6 times, one turn of multiple compression moves the share price about $2.90. From today's 10.2 times, a fall to 9 times prints about $12.60. The stock's own 52-week low is $13.09, against a high of $18.92. The floor has never been tested and there is no mechanism that would stop it breaking.

## 6. RED FLAGS

- The clearing event is supply-negative first. A distribution hands shares to the parent's holders; a monetisation sells them into the market. The parent's own language keeps both doors open - 'the monetization of all or a portion of BHC's ownership interest ... the sale of the Company, the transfer of all or a portion of BHC's remaining ... equity interest ... to its shareholders, or a combination thereof.' If the route is a share offering, 310 million shares meet a 46 million-share float, and offerings that size price at a discount. The event this thesis needs is the same event that first prints a lower price.
- The parent's leverage target is undisclosed, so there is no way to compute how close the condition is to being met.
- Live fraudulent-transfer litigation includes an upheld right to enjoin the share dividend itself, renewable the moment concrete steps are taken.
- The target price is an artefact of a dead process. The $26.97 target sits close to the roughly $25 a share implied by the 2024 private-equity approach, which ended without a transaction eighteen months ago. Wall Street's current average twelve-month target across fourteen analysts is $18.64, with a high of $21 (Citi, raised from $19 in July 2026) and a low of $15; Evercore ISI cut to $16 in July 2026. The consensus rating is neutral - five buys, nine holds, one sell. Our target sits above the street's most bullish case.
- A patent cliff sits at the parent and works against us. Xifaxan faces loss of exclusivity around 2028-2029 with a Medicare price reduction landing in 2027. That erodes the parent's earnings and therefore its leverage ratio, pushing the separation condition further out of reach rather than closer. The parent has said only that an earlier-than-expected loss of exclusivity would force earlier asset monetisation - a route to a distressed sale, not a clean one.
- Pipeline disappointment: a glaucoma candidate recently missed its primary endpoint in a mid-stage trial, and the company announced layoffs in Missouri.

## 7. GREEN FLAGS

- The operating turn is genuine and accelerating: 9% revenue growth in the first quarter, a 59% rise in adjusted earnings, two guidance raises in five months.
- All three segments grew: Vision Care $711 million (+8%), Pharmaceuticals $305 million (+14%), Surgical $228 million (+7%).
- The valuation gap to peers is wide and measurable: an enterprise value near $10.6 billion against $1.035 billion of expected 2026 adjusted earnings is 10.2 times, against roughly 14.4 times for Alcon and 18.5 times for Cooper Companies.
- The subsidiary's own balance sheet is not the bottleneck - it refinanced $2.8 billion of term loans out to January 2031. The constraint sits entirely at the parent.
- The strategic logic is unchanged, and the negative stub at the parent sharpens it. After the Xifaxan cliff, the eye-care stake is the only asset large enough to repair the parent. The event is late, not cancelled.

## 8. VERDICT FOR THE DIRECTOR

On the event, this does not qualify as a dated special situation. There is no clock, the conditions are set and judged by the party that must act, the one live sale attempt died in February 2025, the April 2025 refinancing removed the pressure that would have forced the sponsor's hand, and two legal gates stand in front of the distribution route. Buying this as an event trade means buying an option with no expiry date and paying full carry for it.

On the business, there is a real and improving franchise trading at a genuine discount to its peers - but that is a value case on a two-to-three-year horizon, not a spread that closes on a date.

The single thing to weigh before sizing: the floor is a multiple, not an asset, on equity levered 4.6 times. The 28% fall to $11.80 is as available as the 66% rise to $26.97, and the rise requires an event nobody has scheduled.

On the moat: Bausch + Lomb owns a genuine but narrow intangible-brand and installed-base advantage - a long-established consumer eye-care name, a lens-care franchise, and surgical equipment placed in operating theatres that pulls consumables through. The returns evidence does not support calling it wide: the company still posts losses on a reported basis, carries $4.74 billion of goodwill, and earns a 19% margin against Alcon's roughly 24.5%. Call it narrow and stable. No secular force threatens the terminal value - an ageing population is a tailwind for eye care, not a headwind - so the cheapness is a structure-and-leverage discount rather than a melting base.

# Bausch + Lomb (BLCO) — Event-Driven Dossier

**Setup type:** Forced-seller / divestiture-flow special situation. The thesis is not the eye-care franchise itself; it is the *overhang*. Bausch Health (ticker BHC) still owns about 88% of Bausch + Lomb's shares, a stake it has wanted to sell or spin off since 2020. The bet is that when that block finally clears — through an outright sale of the company or a clean spin-off — the price closes the gap to a strategic-deal value (roughly $25–27 a share) instead of the depressed level (~$16) the market assigns while the parent's debt problems hang over the stock.

## 1. Is the catalyst real, dated, and binding?

This is where the case weakens badly under scrutiny.

- **The catalyst is real but has already failed once.** Bausch Health ran a formal sale process for Bausch + Lomb in 2024, advised by Goldman Sachs, and drew a serious bid: private-equity firms TPG and Blackstone teamed up at a valuation reportedly around $13–14 billion, implying up to about $25 a share. That process was **officially terminated in February 2025** — the company's own statement was that the process "is complete and will not result in a transaction at this time." So the headline event the thesis rests on has been tried and did not happen.
- **What remains is undated and non-binding.** Management still calls full separation "the goal," but there is no signed deal, no record date, no spin effective date, and no scheduled board decision. As of early 2026 there is no public re-launch of a sale. In our terms this is a soft, non-binding catalyst — a stated intention, not a firm, scheduled event with a contractual payout.
- **It is actively blocked, not merely delayed.** The separation cannot proceed unless Bausch Health passes a solvency test after the split, and major creditors — Apollo Global Management, Elliott Management, GoldenTree — have opposed a separation that would strip the eye-care asset away from the debt. This is the core reason the 2024 sale died, and nothing in the 2026 record shows that obstacle cleared.

## 2. Credibility of the sponsor / management on hitting it

Mixed-to-poor on the *event*, even though the operating business is fine. Bausch + Lomb itself is executing — 2025 revenue reached about $5.1 billion across Vision Care (~57%), Pharmaceuticals (~25%) and Surgical (~18%), with new launches (dry-eye, Blink Triple Care) in 2026. But the *decision-maker on the catalyst is not Bausch + Lomb management — it is the parent, Bausch Health, and its creditors.* Bausch Health's credibility on delivering this separation is low: it has signaled the spin since 2020, retained the 88% block for four-plus years, and watched one full sale process collapse. The party that controls the trigger has repeatedly failed to pull it.

## 3. The verified downside floor (what actually backstops the price)

The floor is genuinely real, which is the redeeming feature of the setup. Bausch + Lomb is a profitable, growing, standalone eye-care company — not a melting ice cube. The downside is bounded by its standalone value as an independent business:

- The 52-week low is about $12.06, and the stock has spent 2026 mostly in the $14–17 area on its own operating merits, with the overhang already priced in.
- Analyst consensus sits around $18.25–18.65 (Buy-to-neutral, 11–18 analysts) — i.e., the street already values the standalone business *above* today's price, before any deal premium.
- A reasonable bear/standalone floor is therefore around $11.80–12, roughly the recent low and a discount-to-standalone level that would require the overhang to worsen rather than resolve.

So the loss is bounded by a living business, not by a deal-break to cash. That is the strongest part of the thesis.

## 4. Red flags

- 🔴 **The headline catalyst already misfired** (Feb-2025 process terminated) and has not been re-armed with a date.
- 🔴 **The trigger is controlled by hostile third parties** — the parent's creditors, who have an incentive to *prevent* the clean separation the thesis needs.
- 🔴 **Parent-debt contagion risk:** Bausch Health carries roughly $20 billion of debt with maturities clustering through 2027–2028 and a key drug (Xifaxan) facing generic entry by 2028. A parent restructuring could force a disorderly sale of the BLCO block — which is the bull's catalyst, but could also clear at a discount, not a premium.
- 🟢 **Mitigant:** Bausch + Lomb refinanced its own term loans in January 2026 ($2.8B), so the subsidiary's balance sheet is not the bottleneck — the parent is.
- 🟢 **Mitigant:** the Carl Icahn director arrangement was terminated in August 2025, reducing (not adding) activist noise; there is no live activist process forcing the issue today.

## 5. Verdict on the event

The asymmetry on paper is attractive — about $16 today versus a $25–27 deal value and an ~$12 floor. But the catalyst is the problem: it is undated, non-binding, has already failed once, and is gated on a solvency test that the parent's creditors are blocking. This is a soft, extended catalyst, not a hard, scheduled one. The floor is real (a profitable standalone business near its own fair value), so this is a defensible *patient-value* holding, but it is **not** an imminent, defined-trigger arbitrage. It earns a wait-for-the-catalyst posture, not an aggressive entry, until a sale or spin is actually re-launched with a date.
